notes.text: This layer is prerequisite scaffolding, not a live class, so it gets a short note rather than a full brief.

notes.label: What it covers
notes.text: Python essentials (data types, structures, conditionals, functions, Pandas) and an optional "Hello Agent" mini-project — a CSV FAQ agent built in Streamlit that lets a support user ask questions of a dataframe through an LLM plus a system prompt.
Why it matters: This mini-project introduces the core workflow used throughout the program—business requirement → prompt → model → tool → response.

sections.courseJourney: This is the atom of the entire program: a single agent that thinks, acts, and observes in a loop. It exists because everything later — RAG, multi-agent systems, MCP, fine-tuning — is an elaboration of this one primitive, and none of it makes sense until learners can see an LLM stop being a text box and start being a decision-maker. It sits first because the ReAct loop is the mental model every future module reuses. Each capstone system is, at its core, one or more of these agents wired together.

priorKnowledge.intro: Module 0 — Python essentials (self-paced): variables, data types, operators and strings; lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries; if-else, loops and functions; modules and packages.

sections.learnToday: By the end, learners can: explain what generative models and LLMs actually do and where they fail; write prompts deliberately rather than by trial and error; distinguish a fixed workflow from an autonomous agent; describe the Think–Act–Observe loop and trace it through a running agent; give an agent tools and short/long-term memory; and reason about when a single reflex agent is enough versus when a problem needs planning. They leave able to build a working tool-using agent, evidenced by the IT Support Agent assignment and the CRM Lead Qualifier project.
sections.preparesFor: The agent loop is the spine of the course. Today's ReAct reasoning becomes the retrieval-augmented agent in RAG (W2–W3), the node behavior inside LangGraph (W4), the thing that gets voice and human checkpoints in W5, the client that calls MCP tools (W6), and the unit that gets traced and guardrailed in W8. Tool-calling introduced here is the exact mechanism MCP later standardizes.
connections: When you show the agent loop, remind them the Week 0 FAQ agent answered questions but couldn't choose an action — that gap is what today closes.
When you explain LLM limitations and hallucination, tell them this is precisely the motivation for RAG in two weeks — "we're about to give the agent a memory it can trust."
When you introduce tools, mention that in Week 6 these same tool calls get a universal protocol (MCP) so any agent can use any tool.
When you mention memory (short vs long term), foreshadow that long-term memory is what vector databases (W2) actually store.
When you touch on multi-agent systems as "the future," tell them Week 4 makes that future concrete with LangGraph.
likelyQuestions: "How is an agent different from just prompting ChatGPT well?"
"If the LLM hallucinates, why would I trust an agent built on it?"
"When do I actually need an agent instead of a plain script with if-statements?"
"What's the difference between a workflow and an autonomous agent — isn't a loop just a workflow?"
"Do I have to use LangChain, or can I write the loop myself?"
"How does the agent 'know' which tool to call?"
teachingEmphasis: An agent is a loop, not a single call — Think, Act, Observe, repeat.
Tools are how an LLM touches the real world; without them it can only talk.
LLM limitations (especially hallucination) are features of the terrain, not bugs to be prompted away — they motivate everything downstream.
Autonomy is a spectrum; more autonomy means more need for the guardrails and evaluation coming later.
Prompt engineering is necessary but not sufficient — it's the first tool, not the last.

misconceptions.myth: A good enough prompt removes the need for tools/RAG.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that prompting shapes behavior but cannot inject knowledge the model doesn't have or verify facts — that's why the next four weeks exist.
Clarify that the agent loop is a concept; LangChain is one convenient implementation. They could build it with raw API calls.
Clarify that autonomy trades reliability for flexibility — a theme they'll feel acutely in Week 8.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Your learners arrive knowing Python and how to call an LLM, and maybe having built the Week 0 FAQ agent. Today they cross the line from "prompting a model" to "building an agent" — a reasoning loop that uses tools, keeps memory, and decides its own next step. That's the single most important conceptual jump in the program; protect time for the Think–Act–Observe loop and don't let prompt-engineering tangents eat it. Make sure they leave feeling the limitation that hallucination imposes, because next week you exploit exactly that pain to motivate retrieval. Everything from RAG to multi-agent systems to MCP is this same agent, extended. If they own the loop today, the rest of the course is elaboration; if they don't, every later module will feel like magic instead of engineering.

sections.courseJourney: Last week's agent could reason but only knew what was in its prompt and its training data. This module solves the knowledge problem: how does an agent retrieve the right information from a large private corpus by meaning rather than keyword? It appears now because retrieval is the first real answer to the hallucination pain learners felt in Week 1, and because every serious capstone needs grounded, source-backed answers. This is the "give the agent a reliable memory" week.

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: LLMs and prompting: what Gen AI and LLMs are and where they are used, calling models through client libraries, deliberate prompt engineering, and the limitations of LLMs — hallucination above all.

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: The agent loop: workflows vs autonomous agents; Think–Act–Observe and the ReAct loop; the anatomy of an agent and the three pillars of agency; extending agents with tools; short- vs long-term memory; planning and reasoning; agentic design patterns.

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: Post-class reading: LLM limitations → RAG motivation, LLM hallucinations, a bird's-eye view of Transformers, LangChain, and OpenAI function calling — the RAG-motivation piece sets up today directly. The gap they feel: a fixed prompt cannot scale to a large private knowledge base — their agents only know what fits in the prompt or the model's training data.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: explain why semantic retrieval beats keyword search; turn text into embeddings and reason about similarity; choose and apply chunking strategies (fixed, semantic, recursive, structure-based, LLM-based); store and query vectors in a vector database (Chroma); and pick among indexing strategies (vector, summary, tree, keyword, hybrid) for different query types. They leave able to build the retrieval half of a RAG system, evidenced by the SupportDesk-RAG Part 1 project.
sections.preparesFor: Retrieval built here becomes the R in the full RAG pipeline of W3, the knowledge tool an agent calls in multi-agent systems (W4), and the thing whose quality gets seriously upgraded in Hybrid Search (W7) with sparse/dense vectors and RRF. Chunking and indexing choices made today resurface as tuning knobs in evaluation (W8) and as a core "RAG vs fine-tuning" decision in W9.
connections: Open by reminding them: last week the agent hallucinated because it had no trustworthy source — embeddings are how we build that source.
When you introduce vector databases, stress this is the long-term memory you gestured at in Week 1's memory discussion.
When you compare chunking strategies, tell them chunk quality directly caps retrieval quality — which they'll measure with real metrics in Week 3 and optimize again in Week 7.
When you show indexing strategies, foreshadow that Week 7's hybrid search exists because pure semantic vectors miss exact-match terms.
likelyQuestions: "What's the difference between an embedding and a vector database?"
"How do I choose a chunk size — is there a right answer?"
"Does RAG replace fine-tuning? When would I do one over the other?"
"Why not just stuff the whole document into the context window?"
"How do I know if my retrieval is actually good?"
"Which vector database should I use in production?"
teachingEmphasis: Embeddings are numerical meaning; retrieval is nearest-neighbor search over that meaning.
Chunking is a design decision that silently determines answer quality.
A vector database is infrastructure for storing and searching embeddings — it is not the embedding.
Retrieval is a component you can measure and improve, not a black box.
RAG grounds answers in sources; it is the primary defense against hallucination.

misconceptions.myth: Embeddings and vector databases are the same thing.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify: embeddings are numerical representations of meaning; vector databases store and retrieve them efficiently. This is the single most common confusion at this stage.

misconceptions.myth: Bigger context windows make RAG obsolete.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that cost, latency, and the "lost in the middle" problem keep retrieval essential even with huge windows.
Clarify they solve different problems (knowledge vs behavior) — a distinction Week 9 makes precise.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners come in having felt hallucination as a real limitation last week. Today they get the standard industry answer: retrieve grounded knowledge by semantic similarity. The three ideas that must land are that embeddings encode meaning, that a vector database is just efficient storage-and-search for those embeddings, and that chunking quietly governs everything downstream. Keep the embeddings-vs-vector-DB distinction crisp — it's the misconception that follows learners for weeks. They leave able to retrieve; next week they wrap retrieval into a full pipeline with generation and, crucially, evaluation. Frame today as building the memory, and Week 3 as learning whether the memory is any good.

modules.title: RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents 2 (Pipeline, Evaluation & Agentic RAG)

sections.courseJourney: Week 2 built retrieval; this week turns it into a complete, measurable, and agentic system. It exists because a retrieval demo that works on three documents is not a production RAG system — learners need the full pipeline (indexing + querying), evaluation metrics, and the ability to let an agent decide when and how to retrieve. It sits here because you cannot improve what you cannot measure, and evaluation discipline introduced now pays off in every later module. This is where RAG graduates from "cool demo" to "engineering."

concepts.label: W2
concepts.text: Semantic retrieval: the three critical gaps that motivate semantic retrieval; text embeddings and similarity scoring; storing and querying embeddings in a vector store (post-class: an embeddings + Pinecone notebook and access control for vector databases).

concepts.label: W2
concepts.text: Chunking strategies: fixed-size, semantic, recursive, document-structure-based and LLM-based chunking — and the idea that chunk quality caps retrieval quality.

concepts.label: W2
concepts.text: Indexing and routing: why production RAG keeps multiple indexes (vector, summary, tree, keyword, hybrid), intent-based query routing, and the core retrieval loop "in one picture."

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: Agents and tool-calling: the ReAct loop, tools and memory — the machinery today's Agentic RAG reuses. The gap they feel: they can retrieve, but have no way yet to quantify whether retrieval — or the final answer — is any good.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: assemble a complete RAG pipeline (offline indexing + online querying) with citations, fallback handling, metadata filtering, and conversational memory; evaluate retrieval with Precision/Recall/F1 and generation with groundedness and completeness; and build Agentic RAG with LangChain, where the agent itself decides whether, what, and how many times to retrieve. They leave able to ship and defend a RAG system, evidenced by SupportDesk-RAG Part 2.
sections.preparesFor: The evaluation habits formed here become the backbone of W8 (Observability, Evaluation & Safety) and the LangSmith evaluation step in W9 fine-tuning. Agentic RAG — an agent choosing its retrieval strategy — is the conceptual bridge to multi-agent systems (W4), where routing decisions become explicit. The pipeline structure recurs in the capstone and in the Agentic Research and Text-to-SQL interview deep dives.
connections: Remind them Week 2 gave them retrieval but no way to know if it was good — today's metrics are that missing feedback loop.
When you teach groundedness, connect it straight back to Week 1's hallucination problem: "this metric literally measures how much the model made up."
When you introduce Agentic RAG, note that letting the agent decide to retrieve is a preview of the routing logic in next week's multi-agent systems.
When you cover retrieval metrics, tell them Week 7's hybrid search is one concrete way to move these numbers.
Point out that today's evaluation mindset is the same one they'll apply to whole agent systems in Week 8.
likelyQuestions: "What counts as 'good' Precision or Recall for RAG — is there a benchmark?"
"How is Agentic RAG different from just always retrieving?"
"If my groundedness is low, is it a retrieval problem or a generation problem?"
"Do I need conversational memory for every RAG app?"
"Isn't LLM-as-a-judge circular — using an LLM to grade an LLM?"
"When does RAG stop being enough and I need multiple agents?"
teachingEmphasis: RAG is a two-phase pipeline: offline indexing and online querying — most bugs live at the seam.
You cannot improve retrieval you don't measure; metrics are non-negotiable, not academic.
Groundedness is the direct, quantified answer to hallucination.
Agentic RAG means the agent decides its retrieval strategy — reasoning applied to knowledge.
Low answer quality has two possible root causes (retrieval vs generation); diagnosis matters more than a single score.

misconceptions.myth: High retrieval recall means good answers.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that generation can still fabricate from correct context — retrieval and generation quality are separate axes.

misconceptions.myth: Agentic RAG is just RAG with extra steps.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that the agent's ability to skip, repeat, or reformulate retrieval is a genuine capability jump, not decoration.

misconceptions.myth: Evaluation is a final polish step.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that without evaluation, every improvement afterward is guesswork — this is why it comes now, not at the end.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners arrive able to retrieve but blind to whether their retrieval is any good. Today closes that loop: the full pipeline, real metrics (Precision/Recall/F1, groundedness, completeness), and Agentic RAG where the agent chooses its own retrieval path. The mindset shift — measure, then improve — is the real deliverable and it recurs in Weeks 8 and 9. Make sure they leave able to diagnose whether a bad answer is a retrieval failure or a generation failure, because that diagnostic skill is what separates people who tune RAG from people who guess. Next week the "agent deciding what to do" idea scales up: instead of one agent choosing retrieval, many agents coordinate.

sections.courseJourney: Until now every problem was solved by one agent. This module exists because real systems decompose work across specialized agents — a researcher, a writer, a router — coordinated by explicit state. It appears here because learners have now seen a single agent make routing decisions (Agentic RAG), and the natural next question is "what if the decision is which agent handles this?" LangGraph gives them the graph-and-state machinery to answer that. This is the week the course stops being about agents and starts being about architectures.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: explain why and when to split work across multiple agents; model an application as a LangGraph graph with explicit shared state; build specialized sub-agents and route between them; implement tool-calling loops inside nodes; and reason about orchestration patterns (supervisor/router, specialist agents). They leave able to design and build a coordinated multi-agent system, evidenced by the Travel Planning multi-agent project and the multi-agent content-writer assignment.
sections.preparesFor: LangGraph state is the single most reused artifact from here on. It becomes the foundation for sub-graphs and Human-in-the-Loop (W5), the client side of MCP/A2A orchestration (W6), the thing you trace and evaluate in W8, and the backbone of the capstone and the advanced Multi-Agent Coordination deep dive (W14). If learners don't internalize state today, every later multi-agent topic wobbles.
connections: Frame the jump directly: "Last week one agent decided whether to retrieve; this week we decide which agent should act."
When you introduce LangGraph state, tell them explicitly: "hold onto this — Voice Agents, HITL, MCP orchestration, and your capstone all run on this same state object."
When you show specialist agents, remind them each specialist is just a Week 1 agent — nothing new inside the node, only new wiring between nodes.
When you discuss orchestration overhead, preview Week 8's cost and latency concerns — more agents means more calls to pay for and trace.
Mention that in Week 6 these agents will talk to external agents and tools through standard protocols.
likelyQuestions: "Why can't one clever agent do everything instead of many agents?"
"Is LangGraph mandatory, or can I orchestrate agents myself?"
"What exactly is 'state' and why does it need to be explicit?"
"How do agents pass information to each other?"
"Doesn't adding agents just add cost and latency?"
"How is this different from just calling functions in sequence?"
teachingEmphasis: Multi-agent design is decomposition — split by responsibility, not for its own sake.
Explicit shared state is what makes coordination reliable and debuggable.
Each agent is still a Week-1 loop; the novelty is the graph that connects them.
Orchestration has a cost — more agents means more latency, spend, and failure surface.
A supervisor/router pattern is the workhorse; learn it before exotic topologies.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that every added agent adds coordination cost and new failure modes — decomposition must earn its keep.
Clarify that LangGraph state is a structured, shared object the whole graph reads and writes — far more than a chat log.
Clarify it's a powerful framework, but the underlying idea is a state machine over agents; the concept transfers.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners arrive able to build one capable agent and to let it route its own retrieval. Today they scale that instinct outward: many specialized agents, coordinated through an explicit LangGraph state object. The key realization is that nothing inside a node is new — each node is still last month's agent — and that all the difficulty (and power) lives in the wiring and the shared state. Hammer the state concept, because Voice Agents, Human-in-the-Loop, MCP orchestration, the capstone, and the Week 14 deep dive all sit on top of it. Warn them early that more agents is not free: it buys flexibility with latency, cost, and debugging pain — which is exactly what Week 8 will teach them to manage.

sections.courseJourney: Learners can now coordinate agents, but everything so far has been text and fully autonomous. This module exists to add two things production systems demand: a voice/multimodal interface, and a human checkpoint for high-stakes actions. It sits here because both features are built on top of LangGraph state — you need last week's machinery before you can add sub-graphs and interrupts. This is the week agents become things a real person can talk to and safely supervise.

concepts.text: Multi-agent design: what multi-agent systems are, why and when to build them, the core principle, common workflows and agent patterns, the popular frameworks, and when to use — and not use — sub-agents (post-class reading: Multi-Agent Systems & Orchestration).

concepts.label: W4

W2–W3 — RAG as a callable tool: embeddings, Chroma, the full pipeline, evaluation metrics and Agentic RAG — today's menu and product search agents are RAG tools inside a graph.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: build voice agents (speech-to-text → reasoning → text-to-speech) and reason about the audio stack; compose sub-graphs to modularize complex LangGraph applications; and implement Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) so an agent pauses for human approval or missing information before acting. They leave able to build a supervised, multi-modal conversational system, evidenced by the SnackStack multi-agent food-delivery assignment.
sections.preparesFor: HITL is the conceptual seed of the guardrails and safety work in W8 and the autonomy/safety tradeoffs in the advanced deep dives (W14–W15). Sub-graphs are the modularization pattern learners will reach for in the capstone when a single flat graph becomes unmanageable. Voice and real-time interaction reappear as a design consideration in latency/cost discussions.
connections: Point out that sub-graphs are just last week's graphs nested — "you already know how to build these; now we compose them."
When you introduce HITL, frame it as the first deliberate limit on autonomy — and tell them Week 8 turns this instinct into systematic guardrails.
When you cover voice latency, connect to the cost/latency themes coming in Week 8 and the LLMOps weeks.
Remind them the orchestrator routing to a Menu Agent vs an Order Agent is the same supervisor pattern from Week 4 — only now one branch waits for a human.
Note that a voice agent is still a Week-1 agent loop wearing an audio interface.
likelyQuestions: "When should an agent stop and ask a human versus just act?"
"Do sub-graphs add real value or just complexity?"
"How much latency does voice add, and does it break the experience?"
"Is HITL the same as guardrails?"
"Can I add voice to any of my earlier agents?"
"How does the agent handle being interrupted mid-task?"
teachingEmphasis: Multimodality is an interface layer over the same agent loop — the reasoning doesn't change.
Sub-graphs are modular composition; use them when one graph gets too big to reason about.
HITL is intentional, designed non-autonomy at the points that matter.
Human checkpoints are a reliability tool, not an admission of failure.
Real-time interaction introduces latency budgets you must design around.

misconceptions.myth: Voice agents are a fundamentally different kind of AI.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify they're the same reasoning loop with audio in/out bolted on.

misconceptions.myth: HITL means the agent is just doing what humans tell it.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify HITL is selective — the agent runs autonomously except at defined high-stakes checkpoints.
Clarify they're the standard way to keep complex systems maintainable, which the capstone will demand.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners come in able to orchestrate text agents through LangGraph state. Today they add the two things that make agents deployable to real users: a voice/multimodal interface and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. Emphasize that neither changes the agent's core reasoning — voice is an interface, HITL is a control point — both are built directly on last week's graph and state. The most valuable idea to leave them with is deliberate non-autonomy: choosing where a human must approve. That instinct becomes formal guardrails in Week 8 and mature autonomy tradeoffs in the final deep dives. Next week the agents stop being self-contained and start talking to the outside world — and to each other — through standard protocols.

modules.title: Agent Communication Protocols: MCP, A2A & Google ADK

sections.courseJourney: So far, tools were hand-wired into each agent and agents lived in one codebase. This module exists to standardize two things: how an agent connects to external tools and data (MCP), and how independent agents talk to each other (A2A), with Google ADK as a concrete framework. It appears now because learners have built multi-agent systems (W4) and supervised them (W5) — the next scaling problem is interoperability across systems and vendors. This is the week agents stop being islands.

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: Tool-calling: tools as functions an agent chooses to call, plus OpenAI function calling (post-class reading). Every tool so far has been hand-wired into one agent's code — the friction MCP removes.

concepts.label: W4
concepts.text: Multi-agent orchestration: LangGraph State, routing to specialists, persistence, checkpointers and the Memory Store, and when to use sub-agents.

concepts.label: W5
concepts.text: Voice and sub-graphs: chained ("sandwich") vs speech-to-speech realtime voice architectures; composing sub-graphs — called inside a node or added as a node — with their own persistence.

concepts.label: W5
concepts.text: Human-in-the-loop: pausing a graph with interrupts and resuming it once a human approves or supplies missing information.

concepts.label: W5
concepts.text: Post-class reading: GenAI for Audio — text-to-speech, speaker diarization, WaveNet, voice with LLMs and vocoders.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: explain what MCP standardizes and why (a universal interface between agents and tools/data); build and connect MCP servers, including multiple servers with automatic tool discovery and resilient error handling; implement agent-to-agent (A2A) communication and negotiation; and build multi-agent systems with Google ADK including governance callbacks. They leave able to build interoperable, protocol-based agent systems, evidenced by the MCP/ADK/A2A exercises and the Real Estate Negotiation project.
sections.preparesFor: MCP is the production-standard way learners will connect tools in the capstone and beyond. The governance callbacks introduced here foreshadow guardrails (W8). A2A negotiation is a direct precursor to the Multi-Agent Coordination deep dive (W14), where agent contracts and failure modes get rigorous. Error-handling and self-correction patterns seen here recur in reliability discussions across the LLMOps weeks.
connections: Callback: "In Week 1 you hand-wired tools into the agent. MCP is the industry's answer to doing that once, reusably, for any tool."
When you show multiple MCP servers with tool discovery, connect to Week 4 — "your orchestrator now discovers capabilities instead of hard-coding them."
When you cover A2A negotiation, tell them Week 14 turns this into formal agent roles, contracts, and coordination-failure analysis.
When governance callbacks appear, preview Week 8: "this is guardrails in miniature."
Remind them server failure recovery and LLM self-correction are the same reliability muscle they'll exercise in the LLMOps weeks.
likelyQuestions: "When would I use MCP instead of just calling a function directly?"
"Is MCP replacing LangChain / tool-calling, or complementing it?"
"What's the difference between MCP (agent↔tools) and A2A (agent↔agent)?"
"Do I need Google ADK, or is it one option among many?"
"What happens when an MCP server goes down mid-request?"
"Why do agents need to 'negotiate' — can't they just share data?"
teachingEmphasis: MCP standardizes the agent-to-tool boundary so tools become reusable across agents and vendors.
A2A is a different axis — standardizing agent-to-agent interaction, including negotiation.
Protocols exist to solve scaling and interoperability, not to add ceremony.
Resilient error handling and self-correction are first-class design concerns, not afterthoughts.
Governance callbacks are where safety starts entering the architecture.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify MCP is a standard interface for tools; the agent still calls tools — MCP just makes them portable.

misconceptions.myth: MCP and A2A are the same idea.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify the axes: MCP connects agents to tools/data; A2A connects agents to agents.

misconceptions.myth: Protocols are enterprise overhead I can skip.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that without them, every integration is bespoke and brittle — the pain scales with the system.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners arrive able to build and supervise multi-agent systems inside a single codebase. Today they learn the protocols that let those systems reach outward: MCP for tools and data, A2A for agent-to-agent negotiation, with Google ADK as a working framework. The clarifying distinction to protect is the two axes — MCP (agent↔tools) versus A2A (agent↔agents) — because learners conflate them constantly. Frame protocols as the answer to scaling and interoperability, the natural sequel to last month's orchestration. Governance callbacks here are a quiet preview of Week 8 guardrails, and A2A negotiation is the seed of the Week 14 coordination deep dive. Next week the course pivots back to retrieval quality with hybrid search.

sections.courseJourney: Weeks 2–3 established semantic retrieval, but pure vector search has a blind spot: it misses exact terms, codes, and rare keywords. This module exists to fix retrieval quality by fusing semantic (dense) and lexical (sparse) search. It appears after learners have built and evaluated RAG, because only now do they have the metrics and the felt experience to appreciate why one retrieval method isn't enough. This is the "make retrieval production-grade" week, and it directly moves the numbers learners learned to measure in Week 3.

concepts.label: W2
concepts.text: Dense retrieval: embeddings and similarity, chunking strategies, Chroma, and the five index types (vector, summary, tree, keyword, hybrid) — they have met a hybrid index but not built one from first principles.

concepts.label: W3
concepts.text: Retrieval evaluation: Precision@K, Recall@K and F1@K, K trade-offs, ground-truth setup, groundedness and completeness, LLM-as-judge — the scoreboard today's hybrid search should move. W4–W6 — Retrieval inside larger systems: RAG tools inside LangGraph agents (SnackStack's menu search, AxiomCart's product search) and, most recently, data served to agents through MCP servers.

projects.name: Real Estate Negotiation Workshop
projects.text: Real Estate Negotiation Workshop: autonomous Buyer and Seller agents negotiate property prices using real-time market and inventory data from MCP servers, orchestrated with Google ADK and communicating over A2A.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: distinguish sparse (lexical, e.g. BM25) from dense (semantic) vectors and know when each wins; trace the evolution from keyword search to modern hybrid approaches; combine both retrieval methods and fuse their rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF); and use tools like Qdrant to build a hybrid pipeline. They leave able to build and tune a hybrid retrieval system, evidenced by the PubMedQA biomedical hybrid-search project.
sections.preparesFor: Hybrid search is a concrete lever for the retrieval quality that evaluation (W8) measures and the capstone depends on. The dense/sparse distinction and RRF reappear in the Agentic Research Systems and Text-to-SQL deep dives (W12–W13), where schema and document retrieval must be both precise and semantic. It also sharpens the RAG-vs-fine-tuning reasoning in W9 — sometimes better retrieval, not a new model, is the fix.
connections: Open by returning to a Week 2/3 failure: "Remember when semantic search missed the exact product code? That's the gap sparse vectors fill."
When you teach RRF, tie it back to Week 3 metrics — "this is how we push Recall up without wrecking Precision."
Remind them dense retrieval is exactly the embeddings pipeline from Week 2; they're adding a second, complementary retriever, not replacing the first.
Connect to Week 9: "before you fine-tune to fix bad answers, check whether hybrid retrieval fixes them cheaper."
Note that hybrid retrieval will be a default assumption in the later system-design deep dives.
likelyQuestions: "If embeddings capture meaning, why do we still need keyword search?"
"What is RRF actually doing to combine the two rankings?"
"Is hybrid search always better, or does it depend on the data?"
"Won't running two retrievers double my latency and cost?"
"Does this replace the vector database from Week 2?"
"How do I decide the weighting between sparse and dense?"
teachingEmphasis: Dense and sparse retrieval have complementary strengths — meaning vs exact match.
RRF is a simple, robust way to fuse rankings without tuning fragile weights.
Hybrid search is a quality lever you reach for when metrics stall.
Better retrieval is often a cheaper fix than a bigger model or fine-tuning.
Every added retriever costs latency — quality gains must justify the spend.

misconceptions.myth: Semantic search made keyword search obsolete.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that exact terms, IDs, and rare tokens are where lexical search still wins — hence hybrid.

misconceptions.myth: Hybrid search is a different system from RAG.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify it's an upgrade to the retrieval step inside RAG, not a replacement for it.
Clarify RRF's appeal is that it works well with minimal configuration compared to weighted score fusion.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners arrive having built RAG and, crucially, having measured it — so they know retrieval quality is finite and improvable. Today gives them the strongest single retrieval upgrade in the course: fuse semantic and lexical search with RRF. Anchor the whole session in a concrete Week-2 failure (a missed exact term) so the motivation is visceral, then show how hybrid retrieval moves the exact Precision/Recall numbers they learned in Week 3. The takeaway to leave them with is strategic, not just technical: better retrieval is frequently the cheapest fix — worth checking before reaching for fine-tuning in Week 9. Next week the focus shifts from building capability to making whole systems observable, safe, and affordable.

sections.courseJourney: Learners can now build capable, interoperable, multimodal agent systems — but "it works on my demo" is not "it's safe and affordable in production." This module exists to make systems trustworthy: traceable, measurable, guarded, and cost-controlled. It sits here, right before the production/ops weeks, because it converts the ad-hoc evaluation habits from Week 3 into a systematic discipline applied to entire agent systems. This is the week engineering rigor becomes non-negotiable.

concepts.label: W3
concepts.text: The evaluation mindset: two-layer (retrieval + generation) evaluation, Precision/Recall/F1@K, groundedness and completeness, LLM-as-judge, alert thresholds, a failure-pattern playbook and A/B testing — "measure, then improve." W4–W6 — Systems too complex to debug by eye: LangGraph multi-agent graphs with routing, sub-graphs, checkpointers and interrupts; MCP tool loops across multiple servers; ADK/A2A agents exchanging messages. W5–W6 — Early safety controls: HITL interrupts for high-stakes steps; ADK governance callbacks, prompt-injection defenses and negotiation-stall detection.

concepts.label: W7
concepts.text: Retrieval-quality levers: dense vs sparse vectors, k-NN, ANN and HNSW, inverted indexes and SPLADE, and hybrid search fused with RRF in Qdrant (with FastEmbed).

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: instrument agents for observability (trace and debug multi-step behavior with LangSmith); build evaluation frameworks (custom metrics, golden datasets, LLM-as-judge with DeepEval); implement layered guardrails on inputs and outputs (regex, moderation APIs, Presidio, Guardrails AI, LLM-based checks); and measure and reduce cost. They leave able to operate an agent system responsibly, evidenced by the multi-agent FinTech support project.
sections.preparesFor: This is the direct foundation for LLMOps Part 1 & 2 (W8a, W9a) and the LangSmith evaluation step in fine-tuning (W9). Observability and eval are assumed baseline skills in the capstone and are the entire subject of the Self-Improving Agents deep dive (W15). Cost optimization reasoning recurs in every "which model / how big a GPU" decision later.
connections: Callback: "In Week 3 you evaluated retrieval; today you evaluate the whole agent system — same mindset, bigger scope."
When you show tracing, remind them how painful debugging felt in Week 4's multi-agent project — tracing is the cure.
When you teach guardrails, connect to Week 5 HITL and Week 6 governance callbacks: "those were early instincts; this is the systematic version."
When you cover cost, tie it back to Week 4's warning that more agents means more spend — now they can measure it.
Preview that Week 15's entire deep dive is about agents evaluating and improving themselves using exactly these tools.
likelyQuestions: "Isn't using an LLM to judge an LLM (LLM-as-judge) circular?"
"How many guardrails is enough — where do I stop?"
"What's the difference between observability and evaluation?"
"How do I build a golden dataset if I don't have labeled data?"
"Where is most of my cost actually going in a multi-agent system?"
"Do guardrails hurt latency and user experience?"
teachingEmphasis: Observability (what happened) and evaluation (was it good) are distinct and both required.
Guardrails are layered — input and output, multiple techniques — not a single filter.
Evaluation needs a reference: golden datasets and clear metrics beat vibes.
Cost is an engineering metric you design against, not a surprise on the invoice.
Trustworthiness is built in, through instrumentation, not bolted on at the end.

misconceptions.myth: LLM-as-judge is unreliable because it's circular.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that a judge with a rubric, examples, and a different role than the generator is a validated, widely-used technique — imperfect but far better than nothing.

misconceptions.myth: Observability and evaluation are the same.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify: observability tells you what the agent did; evaluation tells you whether it was good.
Clarify they also cover format validation, PII, injection defense, and business-rule enforcement.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners arrive able to build powerful systems that are hard to trust or debug. Today is where the program's engineering conscience lands: trace everything, evaluate systematically, guard inputs and outputs, and measure cost. The mindset from Week 3 (measure then improve) now applies to whole agent systems. Keep the observability-vs-evaluation distinction sharp, and address the LLM-as-judge skepticism head-on — it's the objection that derails this class. Everything from here is about operating systems well: the two LLMOps inserts, the fine-tuning evaluation, and the capstone all assume these skills. Frame today as the transition from "can I build it?" to "can I run it responsibly and afford it?"

sections.courseJourney: This short insert exists to give learners the operational vocabulary that Weeks 8 through 9 assume: what "Ops" means, how MLOps evolved, and how LLMOps differs. It sits immediately after observability/evaluation because those are the raw materials of an ops practice. It moves learners toward the capstone by reframing everything they've built as a system to be operated, not just a program to be run.

concepts.label: W8

W4–W7 — End-to-end agent systems: LangGraph orchestration, voice and HITL, MCP/ADK/A2A and hybrid retrieval — the kinds of systems an ops practice must run.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: articulate the "Ops mindset" (reliability, repeatability, monitoring, iteration); explain what MLOps established and why; and describe how LLMOps extends and differs from classic MLOps (prompts as artifacts, non-determinism, eval-driven deployment). They leave able to talk about their systems in production/operational terms, grounded by a demo.
sections.preparesFor: This vocabulary is the frame for W9 fine-tuning (which needs deployment/versioning thinking) and LLMOps Part 2 (W9a). It shapes how learners reason about the capstone as a deployable, maintainable system and underpins the productionization phases in the later deep dives.
connections: Connect to Week 8: "the traces, evals, and cost metrics you just learned are the instruments an ops practice runs on."
Contrast with traditional software ops learners may know: "same discipline, new failure modes — non-determinism and prompt drift."
Foreshadow Week 9: "you can't fine-tune responsibly without versioning and deployment discipline — that's LLMOps."
Note that the capstone's grade partly reflects whether it's built like something operable, not just demo-able.
likelyQuestions: "How is LLMOps different from the DevOps/MLOps I already know?"
"Why is non-determinism such a big deal operationally?"
"Is a prompt really an 'artifact' I need to version?"
"Do I need all this ops machinery for a small project?"
"Where does evaluation fit in a deployment pipeline?"
teachingEmphasis: Ops is a mindset — reliability, monitoring, iteration — before it's tooling.
LLMOps inherits from MLOps but adds non-determinism and prompt/version management.
Evaluation is part of the deployment loop, not a separate activity.
Prompts, datasets, and eval suites are versioned artifacts.
"It runs" and "it's operable" are different bars.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify the genuinely new problems: non-determinism, prompt/version drift, eval-gated releases.

misconceptions.myth: Ops is only for large teams.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify the mindset scales down; even a solo project benefits from monitoring and versioned prompts.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This is a short framing module: give learners the operational language to describe what they've built. They arrive fluent in building and evaluating agents; today they learn to see those agents as systems that must be deployed, monitored, and iterated — the Ops mindset, MLOps lineage, and what LLMOps adds on top. The one idea to leave them with is that evaluation is part of the release loop, not a final polish. This sets up fine-tuning next week (which demands versioning and deployment discipline) and the capstone's expectation that systems be operable, not just demoable.

sections.courseJourney: Every previous fix changed the system around the model — better prompts, retrieval, orchestration, guardrails. This module exists for the cases those can't solve: when you need to change the model's behavior itself. It appears late deliberately, so learners first exhaust the cheaper levers (prompting, RAG, hybrid search) and can reason about when fine-tuning is actually the right tool. This is the "reach into the model" week, and it closes the technical arc before the capstone.

priorKnowledge.intro: W2–W3, W7 — Knowledge levers: RAG (embeddings, chunking, Chroma, pipelines, Agentic RAG) and hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse vectors, SPLADE, HNSW, RRF in Qdrant) — the cheaper fixes to rule out before training.

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: Prompt engineering: the first of the three domain-adaptation approaches (prompting, RAG, fine-tuning) compared today. W3, W8 — Evaluation: RAG metrics, LangSmith datasets and custom evaluators, LLM-as-judge, A/B experiments and DeepEval/G-Eval — today's "metrics over vibes" step reuses them directly.

concepts.label: W8
concepts.text: Cost economics: token economics, before/after measurement and the cost–quality Pareto frontier.

concepts.label: W8(a)

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: audit and prepare datasets and judge data quality before training; run QLoRA fine-tuning (e.g. on Colab); deploy and serve adapters efficiently (HF, adapter toggling with no extra VRAM); and evaluate fine-tuned vs base models with LangSmith ("metrics over vibes"); plus estimate deployment cost. They leave able to decide on, execute, and evaluate a fine-tune, evidenced by the fine-tuning project.
sections.preparesFor: Fine-tuning completes the learner's decision toolkit for the capstone: prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune. The dataset-quality and QLoRA reasoning underpin LLMOps Part 2 (W9a) and the optimization/model-selection thinking in the deep dives. The base-vs-fine-tuned evaluation discipline is a direct application of Week 8's evaluation frameworks.
connections: Frame the whole module as a decision: "Weeks 2, 3, and 7 were about knowledge; today is about behavior. Ask which one your problem needs before you train."
Callback to Week 7: "before fine-tuning to fix bad answers, did hybrid retrieval already fix them cheaper?"
Tie "metrics over vibes" straight to Week 8: "same evaluation frameworks, now comparing two models."
Connect QLoRA/adapters to Week 8a's cost and deployment concerns.
Preview that model selection and GPU sizing get revisited in the optimization deep dives.
likelyQuestions: "When do I fine-tune instead of using RAG or better prompts?"
"What is QLoRA and why does it make fine-tuning affordable?"
"How much data do I actually need, and how good does it have to be?"
"Will fine-tuning make the model forget things (catastrophic forgetting)?"
"How do I prove the fine-tuned model is actually better?"
"What does it cost to serve a fine-tuned model in production?"
teachingEmphasis: Fine-tuning changes behavior/style, not knowledge — RAG is still the tool for knowledge.
Data quality dominates outcomes — audit before you train.
QLoRA/adapters make fine-tuning cheap enough to be a real option, not just a research luxury.
Base-vs-fine-tuned must be settled with metrics, not impressions.
Fine-tuning is one tool in a decision hierarchy — usually the last one to reach for.

misconceptions.myth: Fine-tuning is how you add knowledge to a model.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that fine-tuning teaches behavior/format/style; for facts, use retrieval. This is the pivotal distinction of the module.
Clarify that a small, clean, well-targeted dataset often beats a large noisy one.

misconceptions.myth: Fine-tuning is too expensive/advanced for real projects.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that QLoRA and adapters have made it broadly accessible.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners arrive having fixed problems by improving the system around the model. Today they learn to change the model itself — and, more importantly, when that's the right move. Protect the central distinction: fine-tuning shapes behavior and style; RAG supplies knowledge. Reinforce that data quality, not volume, decides success, and that QLoRA/adapters make this a practical, affordable option. Everything connects to earlier weeks: it's a decision built on top of prompting, RAG, and hybrid search, evaluated with Week 8's frameworks, deployed with Week 8a's discipline. This closes the technical curriculum — next comes the capstone, where all these levers get used together on one shipped system.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: apply AgentOps practices to multi-step agent systems; treat evals & quality as a continuous, gating process; design for reliability (retries, fallbacks, failure isolation) and manage cost at scale. They leave with a mental production-readiness checklist, grounded by a demo.
sections.preparesFor: Directly de-risks the capstone and defines what "production-ready" means for it. The reliability and cost themes are load-bearing in every advanced deep dive (W12–W15), where productionization is an explicit phase.
connections: Tie together the whole trust arc: "Week 8 gave you the instruments, 8a the mindset, today the checklist."
Connect reliability patterns to Week 6's server-failure recovery and self-correction — "same instincts, system-wide now."
Frame cost-at-scale as the grown-up version of Week 4's "more agents cost more."
Tell them explicitly: "your capstone will be judged partly on these production concerns."
likelyQuestions: "What does 'production-ready' actually mean for an agent?"
"How do I make a non-deterministic system reliable?"
"How often should evals run — every deploy, continuously?"
"What's the biggest cost trap in agent systems at scale?"
"How is AgentOps different from the LLMOps we just covered?"
teachingEmphasis: Reliability for agents means designing for failure — retries, fallbacks, isolation.
Evals are continuous and gating, not one-time.
Cost management is an architectural concern at scale.
AgentOps applies ops discipline to multi-step, non-deterministic systems.
Production readiness is a checklist you can articulate and defend.

misconceptions.myth: If it passes evals once, it's production-ready.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that quality drifts; evals must run continuously.
Clarify it's about system design — fallbacks, retries, graceful degradation.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This short capstone-launch module consolidates the trust arc into production readiness for agents: AgentOps, continuous evals, reliability, and cost at scale. Learners arrive with the instruments (Week 8), the mindset (8a), and fine-tuning experience (Week 9); today they get the checklist that ties it together. The one idea to leave them with is that reliability in a non-deterministic system is a design problem — retries, fallbacks, isolation — not a prompting problem. Send them into the capstone thinking like operators. Everything they build over the next two weeks should be defensible against these production concerns.

sections.courseJourney: The capstone exists to force integration: nine weeks of separately-taught capabilities must now fuse into one coherent, operable system. It sits here because learners finally hold the full toolkit — agents, RAG, orchestration, protocols, evaluation, ops, fine-tuning — and the only way to prove mastery is to ship. It's the bridge between "learned the pieces" and "can build a system," and the reference point the later interview deep dives assume.

sections.preparesFor: The capstone is the concrete artifact the interview-prep deep dives (W12–W15) abstract from. Every design decision made here — coordination, verification, retrieval, productionization — is exactly what those sessions rehearse at whiteboard/interview depth. It's also the primary portfolio piece for job search.

Frame the capstone as interview material: "you'll re-tell these decisions in Weeks 12–15 as system-design answers."

teachingEmphasis: Architecture is a series of justified decisions, not a pile of features.
Use the least powerful tool that solves the problem (prompt < RAG < multi-agent < fine-tune).
Observability and evaluation are part of the deliverable, not extras.
Cost and reliability tradeoffs must be explicit and defensible.
The story of why you built it this way matters as much as the demo.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that unjustified complexity is a negative signal; restraint and rationale win.
Clarify that decisions, evaluation, and operability are what distinguish a strong capstone.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This is integration under pressure. Learners hold the whole toolkit and must now fuse it into one operable system and — just as importantly — justify every choice. Your highest-value coaching is forcing rationale: why this architecture, why RAG over fine-tuning, where the guardrails and evals are, what it costs. Redirect "make it smarter" instincts back to retrieval and evaluation rather than more prompting or more agents. Remind them the capstone isn't just a portfolio demo — it's the raw material they'll narrate as senior-level system-design answers in the next four weeks. Reward restraint and defensible decisions over feature count. SWE Interview-Prep Deep Dives (Weeks 12–15) These four modules are structured as phased system-design walkthroughs — the format of a senior AI-engineering interview. They exist to convert everything learners built in the capstone into everything they can reason about aloud under questioning. They are shared verbatim with the EM track.

modules.title: Agentic Research Systems: Planning, Tools & Guardrails

sections.courseJourney: This deep dive exists to rehearse designing a research agent — one that plans multi-step investigations, uses tools, remembers, and stays guarded — at interview depth. It comes after the capstone because it presumes learners can already build such systems; now they practice defending the design. It moves them toward the job-search finish line, where system-design fluency, not just working code, is what's assessed.

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: Planning and the agent loop: ReAct, planning and reasoning, agentic design patterns — today's refresh extends these to Plan-and-Execute, hybrids, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts and CodeAct. W1, W6 — Tools: function calling and MCP (primitives, transports, multiple servers, automatic tool discovery, failure recovery and LLM self-correction). W2–W3, W7 — Retrieval: embeddings, chunking, indexing, RAG evaluation, and hybrid dense + sparse search with RRF — the research agent's retrieval module. W1, W4 — Memory: short- vs long-term memory, LangGraph checkpointers and the Memory Store. W8, W8(a), W9(a) — Trust and production: tracing, evaluators, LLM-as-judge, layered guardrails including prompt-injection detection, and cost tracking; retries, circuit breakers, fallback chains and graceful degradation.

projects.label: Project
projects.name: Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System
projects.text: Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System: answered travel questions with deep research and ran multiple queries in parallel — the closest earlier build to a research agent.

projects.label: Project
projects.name: Multi-Agent FinTech Support System
projects.text: Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: a traced, evaluated, guarded multi-agent system — their reference for Phase 4 (observability + feedback) and Phase 5 (testing).

projects.label: Project
projects.name: SupportDesk-RAG Part 2

sections.learnToday: Working through six phases — fundamentals refresh, system design, memory design, observability + feedback, testing strategy, productionization — learners will be able to: architect a research agent from a blank prompt; justify memory and tool choices; design guardrails and feedback loops; and articulate a productionization path. They leave able to whiteboard a research-agent design end to end.
sections.preparesFor: This is terminal interview preparation, but it also reinforces patterns reused in Text-to-SQL (W13) and Multi-Agent Coordination (W14) — planning, tool design, and guardrails are shared vocabulary across all three.

Tie memory design to Week 2's short/long-term memory and vector stores.
Tie guardrails and feedback to Week 8's observability and evaluation.
Frame productionization against LLMOps (W8a/9a).
Note that the phase structure itself is a reusable interview framework.

"How do I choose memory architecture on the spot?"

"What's a strong answer for 'how would you productionize this'?"
teachingEmphasis: System design is a structured conversation — the phases are a framework, not a script.
Every choice needs a stated tradeoff.
Memory and guardrails are where weak candidates go silent — over-prepare them.
Feedback loops distinguish a toy from a system.
Productionization thinking signals seniority.

misconceptions.myth: System design is about naming tools.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify it's about justified tradeoffs and failure handling.

misconceptions.myth: A research agent is just RAG.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify it adds planning, multi-step tool use, and iterative refinement.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Learners arrive able to build research agents; this session makes them able to defend the design under interview pressure. Walk the six phases as a reusable framework and force a stated tradeoff at every step, especially on memory and guardrails, where candidates typically stall. Anchor everything to concrete capstone decisions so it's recall, not invention. The goal isn't new capability — it's fluency and structure. This is the first of four interview rehearsals; the planning/tools/guardrails vocabulary here recurs across the next three.

modules.title: Agentic Text-to-SQL: Reliable Data Reasoning Systems

sections.courseJourney: This deep dive tackles one of the hardest, most-asked interview problems: an agent that turns natural language into reliable SQL over real schemas. It exists because Text-to-SQL concentrates almost every course theme — retrieval (schema), sub-agents, tool design, guardrails, self-correction, evaluation — into one high-stakes problem where being wrong is worse than being silent. It comes late because it assumes command of all those pieces.

concepts.label: W7
concepts.text: Hybrid retrieval: sparse (inverted index, SPLADE) and dense vectors fused with RRF — today's schema retrieval combines BM25 and dense embeddings with other signals in a five-signal funnel.

concepts.label: W4
concepts.text: Sub-agents and LangGraph state machines: routing, sub-agents and when not to use them — the basis for today's sub-agent topology and self-correction state machine.

concepts.label: W6
concepts.text: MCP and self-correction: MCP servers and tool contracts, server-failure recovery and LLM self-correction — today's execute_sql tool sits behind read-only and read-write MCP servers.

concepts.label: W8
concepts.text: Guardrails, evaluation and cost: layered guardrails and injection defense, LLM-as-judge, CI/CD evals and cost tracking.

concepts.label: W12
concepts.text: Deep dive: Agentic Research Systems: the phased interview framework; ReAct vs Plan-and-Execute; tool failure modes; layered prompt-injection defense; memory trade-offs; the limits of LLM-as-judge; and productionization (invocation patterns, circuit breakers, caching).

projects.label: Project
projects.name: Multi-Agent FinTech Support System
projects.text: Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: layered guardrails and custom evaluators — the base for today's AST validator, policy-as-code checks and CI eval gate.

projects.name: MCP exercises

sections.learnToday: Across nine phases (framing, pipeline & cost math, schema retrieval, semantic layer & sub-agent topology, tool design, guardrails, self-correction & retry, evaluation & observability, productionization at scale), learners will be able to: design a Text-to-SQL system that retrieves the right schema, decomposes work across sub-agents, guards against unsafe/incorrect queries, self-corrects on failure, and is evaluated and cost-modeled. They leave able to defend a production-grade data-reasoning system.
sections.preparesFor: Terminal interview prep. It also crystallizes the self-correction/retry pattern that the Self-Improving Agents deep dive (W15) generalizes, and the schema retrieval pattern that reuses hybrid search from W7.
connections: Tie schema retrieval directly to Week 7 hybrid search: "exact table/column names are a lexical-match problem."
Connect sub-agent topology to Week 4 orchestration.
Tie guardrails to Week 8 and to the cost of a wrong query executing against production data.
Connect self-correction to Week 6's LLM self-correction patterns.
Frame the cost math phase against LLMOps cost thinking.
likelyQuestions: "Why is Text-to-SQL so much harder than normal RAG?"
"How does the agent retrieve the right schema without loading the whole database?"
"What guardrails stop a destructive or wrong query?"
"How does self-correction work when the SQL fails?"
"How do I evaluate correctness when there are many valid queries?"
teachingEmphasis: Reliability is the whole game — a confidently wrong query is the worst outcome.
Schema retrieval is a retrieval problem (and hybrid search shines here).
Sub-agent decomposition tames complexity.
Self-correction/retry turns failures into recoveries.
Correctness evaluation is subtle — multiple valid answers exist.

misconceptions.myth: Text-to-SQL is just prompting the model with the schema.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify why schema retrieval, guardrails, and self-correction are essential at real scale.

misconceptions.myth: If the SQL runs, it's correct.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that executable and correct are different — evaluation must check semantics.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: Text-to-SQL is the course's capstone problem in miniature — retrieval, sub-agents, guardrails, self-correction, evaluation, and cost, all under a strict reliability bar. Learners arrive with every piece; today they assemble and defend them for a problem where being wrong beats being silent only in the sense that both are failures. Anchor schema retrieval to Week 7 hybrid search and self-correction to Week 6. The nine phases are dense — prioritize framing, schema retrieval, guardrails, and self-correction if time is short. Emphasize that reliability, not cleverness, is what interviewers probe. Next up: coordinating many agents.

sections.courseJourney: Week 4 taught learners to build multi-agent systems; this deep dive teaches them to reason rigorously about coordination — roles, contracts, topology, shared state, and the failure modes that emerge when agents depend on each other. It exists because "add more agents" is where naive designs break, and interviewers probe exactly that. It comes late because it presumes fluency with orchestration, MCP/A2A, and reliability.

concepts.label: W4
concepts.text: LangGraph multi-agent systems: State, persistence, the Memory Store, supervisor/router patterns, sub-agents and when not to use them.

concepts.label: W5
concepts.text: Sub-graphs and HITL: composing sub-graphs and pausing on interrupts for human approval — the seed of today's "HITL on every destructive action."

concepts.label: W6
concepts.text: A2A and Google ADK: Agent Cards, context threading, parts and artifacts; Sequential, Parallel and Loop agents, Agent-as-Tool and callbacks; negotiation orchestration under information asymmetry. W8, W9(a) — Reliability, cost and evaluation: retries, timeouts and circuit breakers, fallback chains, graceful degradation, rate limiting and budget caps; per-agent tracing and routing-accuracy evaluators. W12–W13 — Deep dives 1–2: the eight-stage interview framework (restate, requirements, topology, tools, failure modes, eval, scaling, trade-offs); Plan-and-Execute vs ReAct; sub-agent topology and model selection; self-consistency; six-layer defense in depth.

projects.name: AxiomCart

sections.learnToday: Across its phases (clarify, architecture, coordination via agent roles & contracts, coordination topology, shared intelligence, reliability/execution, coordination failure modes, scale, production concerns, tradeoffs), learners will be able to: define agent roles and contracts; choose a coordination topology; design shared intelligence/state; and anticipate and mitigate coordination failure modes at scale. They leave able to defend a multi-agent architecture — including where it shouldn't be multi-agent.
sections.preparesFor: Terminal interview prep. Consolidates the multi-agent thread that began at W4 and ran through A2A (W6), and pairs with Self-Improving Agents (W15) as the two "advanced systems" interviews.
connections: Callback to Week 4: "you built these; now define the contracts between them."
Tie A2A negotiation (W6) to formal coordination topology here.
Connect failure modes to Week 8/9a reliability.
Repeatedly ask "would a single agent be simpler?" — the strongest answers know when not to go multi-agent.
Frame shared intelligence as the grown-up version of LangGraph state.
likelyQuestions: "When is multi-agent genuinely better than one strong agent?"
"What's an 'agent contract' and why does it matter?"
"How do coordination failures actually happen?"
"How do agents share state reliably at scale?"
"How do I discuss tradeoffs without sounding hand-wavy?"
teachingEmphasis: Coordination needs explicit roles and contracts, not vibes.
Topology is a design choice with real consequences.
Multi-agent systems fail in new ways — plan for coordination failure.
Knowing when not to use multi-agent is a seniority signal.
Shared intelligence is disciplined shared state.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify the coordination tax and failure surface; sometimes one agent wins.
Clarify that contracts, topology, and shared state are deliberately engineered.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This is the rigorous sequel to Week 4. Learners can already wire agents together; today they reason about roles, contracts, topology, shared intelligence, and — the part interviews love — coordination failure modes. The single most valuable habit to instill is asking "would one agent be simpler?" before defending a multi-agent design; candidates who default to more agents look junior. Anchor to Week 4 state and Week 6 A2A. Emphasize that multi-agent systems fail in ways single agents don't, and that anticipating those failures is what separates a strong answer from a feature list. One deep dive remains: agents that evaluate and improve themselves.

sections.courseJourney: The final deep dive closes the loop the whole course has been building toward: agents that verify their own work and improve. Using a code-review system as the anchor, it generalizes evaluation (W3, W8) into verification loops, LLM-as-judge, and online/offline feedback. It exists because self-verification is the frontier of reliable agentic systems and a favorite hard interview topic. It's last because it requires mastery of evaluation, reliability, and multi-agent design.

priorKnowledge.intro: W3, W8 — Evaluation: Precision/Recall/F1, groundedness, LLM-as-judge (faithfulness, correctness), custom evaluators, MRR, A/B experiments and hill-climbing, DeepEval/G-Eval in CI/CD.

concepts.label: W9
concepts.text: Before/after evaluation: base vs fine-tuned comparisons with LangSmith evaluators for helpfulness, accuracy and safety — including a real regression.

concepts.label: W9(a)
concepts.text: Continuous evals: task- vs system-level evaluation, automated vs human review, regression testing in CI/CD, golden and synthetic datasets, and the trust scorecard.

concepts.label: W13
concepts.text: Verification in miniature: AST validation, dry-run/EXPLAIN, self-consistency (choosing K), monthly LLM-judge calibration and CI eval gates.

concepts.label: W14
concepts.text: Coordination: role contracts, supervisor topology, typed shared state and the Critic as an online judge — today's "reviewers as a multi-agent system" builds directly on it.

projects.name: Multi-Agent FinTech Support System
projects.text: Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: custom evaluators (routing_accuracy, keyword_correctness), LLM-as-judge for faithfulness and correctness, and DeepEval in CI — the offline-evaluation half of today's design.

SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: where "measure, then improve" started; today's golden dataset and per-category precision/recall are the same ideas at production scale. Capstone: each learner's own evaluation and observability plan.
Callback: ask what theirs caught — and what it missed.

sections.learnToday: Across its phases (clarify, architecture, context & grounding, the reviewers, signal fusion, why verification is hard, offline evaluation, the verification loop, verifying correctness, LLM-as-judge, online evaluation & feedback, reliability & scale, tradeoffs), learners will be able to: design multiple reviewer agents, fuse their signals, build offline and online verification loops, use LLM-as-judge responsibly, and reason about why verification is genuinely hard. They leave able to defend a self-improving agent architecture.
sections.preparesFor: Terminal interview prep and the conceptual summit of the program — it ties evaluation, multi-agent design, and reliability into one system. Nothing depends on it downstream; it's the capstone of the interview sequence.
connections: Frame it as the natural end of the evaluation thread from Week 3 and Week 8.
Tie multiple reviewers + signal fusion to Week 14 coordination.
Revisit the LLM-as-judge skepticism from Week 8 and resolve it with rubric/grounding techniques.
Connect online feedback to LLMOps continuous-eval thinking.
Emphasize honesty about verification's limits — a mature, senior stance.

"Isn't LLM-as-judge circular — again?"
"What's the difference between offline and online evaluation here?"
"Why is verification harder than generation?"
"How do I fuse disagreeing reviewer signals?"
teachingEmphasis: Verification is harder than generation — respect that difficulty.
Multiple reviewers plus signal fusion beat a single judge.
Grounding and rubrics make LLM-as-judge defensible.
Offline and online evaluation play different roles.
Self-improvement is a loop: verify, learn, iterate.

misconceptions.myth: An agent can just check its own work.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify why naive self-checking fails and why grounded, multi-signal verification is needed.
Clarify that with rubrics, grounding, and multiple judges it's a legitimate, widely-used technique.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This is the program's conceptual summit: agents that verify and improve themselves. Learners arrive fluent in evaluation, multi-agent design, and reliability; today those threads converge into verification loops, multiple reviewers with signal fusion, LLM-as-judge done responsibly, and honest treatment of why verification is hard. Resolve the recurring LLM-as-judge skepticism decisively here. The senior stance to leave them with is intellectual honesty about verification's limits paired with concrete techniques to push past them. This completes the interview sequence — from here, learners are rehearsing, not learning. Send them out able to defend the hardest system in the course. TRACK 2 — Engineering Managers (EMs) The arc: EMs learn the same agentic mental model as SWEs but build it in n8n (visual, no-code) so they can reason about, evaluate, and lead agentic projects without living in the code. The path runs from a single reflex agent (W1) → grounded RAG agents (W2) → orchestrated multi-agent systems with a critic (W3) → voice/conversational agents (W4) → workflow integration via MCP/A2A/Skills (W5) → evaluation and operations (W6) → optimization and fine-tuning economics (W7), with LLMOps inserts, a capstone, and the same four senior system-design deep dives as SWEs. The emphasis throughout is judgment — when to use what, and what it costs — over implementation detail.

notes.text: Prerequisite scaffolding, not a live class.

notes.label: What it covers
notes.text: "Python for Non-Programmers" plus an optional AI exercise. The goal is literacy, not fluency — enough to read a workflow and reason about logic, not to ship production code.

Why it matters to you as an instructor: EMs often arrive rusty or non-coding. Set expectations early: they don't need to write much Python, but they must be able to follow logic, data flow, and conditionals, because every n8n workflow encodes exactly those. When workflows get complex in Weeks 3–5, learners who skipped this struggle to reason about branching and state. Frame Python literacy as the language for thinking about systems they'll build visually.

sections.courseJourney: This is the atom of the program for EMs: the leap from a fixed rule to a reasoning agent, built visually in n8n. It exists so managers can see what an agent is — a loop that evaluates, decides, and acts — rather than treat it as a buzzword. It's first because every later module (RAG, orchestration, ops) is an extension of this loop, and because leading agentic teams starts with understanding the primitive.

priorKnowledge.intro: Module 0 — Python for Non-Programmers (self-paced): basics, NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib — enough literacy to follow logic, data flow and conditionals, the same constructs every n8n workflow encodes. Literacy, not fluency.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: explain generative AI and LLMs and where they fail; write deliberate prompts; distinguish reflex/rule-based behavior from reasoning agents; and build a working agent in n8n that evaluates severity, maintains state to avoid duplicates, and emits structured decisions. Evidenced by the E-commerce Operations Agent that monitors checkout failures and publishes ALERT/LOG decisions via webhook.
sections.preparesFor: The agent loop underpins RAG (W2), orchestration (W3), conversational agents (W4), and everything after. State management introduced here (avoiding duplicate processing) recurs in every workflow. The "map a business requirement to agent steps" instinct is the core managerial skill the whole track builds.
connections: Frame the reflex→reasoning jump as the difference between automation they already know and the agents they'll lead.
When you show state, note it recurs everywhere — "every workflow you build will manage state like this."
Foreshadow RAG: "this agent only knows its inputs; next week we give it a knowledge base."
Tie hallucination to why evaluation (W6) and guardrails exist.
Connect n8n nodes to the conceptual agent loop so the tool doesn't obscure the idea.
likelyQuestions: "As a manager, how much of this do I need to build myself?"
"How is an agent different from the automation/Zapier we already use?"
"When is an agent overkill versus a simple rule?"
"Can I trust an agent to make decisions autonomously?"
"Why n8n instead of writing code?"
teachingEmphasis: An agent is a reasoning loop, not a fancy if-statement.
State management is fundamental, not advanced.
Business requirement → agent steps is the core skill.
LLM limitations (hallucination) motivate everything downstream.
Visual tools reveal the architecture; the concepts are what transfer.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify that reasoning and autonomous decision-making are a real category shift from rule-based flows.
Clarify that n8n workflows still embody real design decisions.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: EMs arrive with product-level AI awareness but often little hands-on exposure. Today they build their first reasoning agent visually and, more importantly, learn to see the agent loop beneath the buzzwords. Keep them focused on the concept — evaluate, decide, act, remember — rather than n8n mechanics, and make sure they leave able to map a business need to agent steps. That translation skill is what makes them effective leaders of agentic projects. Plant the hallucination pain now; it's the seed for RAG next week and evaluation later. Everything ahead extends this single loop.

sections.courseJourney: Last week's agent knew only its inputs. This module gives it grounded knowledge via retrieval, so it can answer from a real corpus rather than guess. It exists because most business agents EMs will oversee are fundamentally RAG systems, and managers must understand retrieval's moving parts to evaluate them. It's positioned right after the agent loop because grounding is the first and most important capability upgrade.

concepts.text: Gen AI and LLM fundamentals: the evolution of AI, the SDLC becoming AI-driven, what Gen AI and LLMs are, prompt engineering, and the limitations of LLMs — hallucination above all.

concepts.label: W1
concepts.text: Agents: agents and tools, agentic workflows vs autonomous agents, how EMs can leverage agents, and two design patterns: reflection and routing.

concepts.label: W1

The gap they feel: their agent can only judge the data it is handed — it has no access to past incidents, policies or documents.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: explain RAG and why it beats keyword search; reason about chunking and metadata design; understand embeddings and vector databases conceptually; ensure grounded responses via context injection; and build a RAG agent in n8n. Evidenced by the AI Finance Reporting Agent that retrieves from a vector DB, blends internal and external data, and emails a leadership report.

connections: Callback to Week 1: "the agent hallucinated because it had no source — RAG is the fix."
Keep embeddings-vs-vector-DB crisp; it's the classic confusion.
Note chunking/metadata quality caps answer quality — which they'll measure in Week 6.
Frame grounding as the manager's main lever for trustworthy outputs.

"How do I judge if a team's RAG system is any good?"
"Does RAG replace fine-tuning?"
"Why not just paste everything into the prompt?"
"How much does metadata design actually matter?"
teachingEmphasis: RAG grounds answers in sources — the main defense against hallucination.
Embeddings encode meaning; vector databases store and search them (not the same thing).
Chunking and metadata quietly govern quality.
Grounding is a leadership lever for trust.
Retrieval quality is measurable — a theme for Week 6.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify the distinction explicitly.
Clarify: knowledge vs behavior — different problems.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: EMs come in having felt hallucination in their first agent. Today they learn the industry's standard remedy — retrieval-augmented generation — and how to reason about its parts well enough to evaluate a team's system. Keep the embeddings-vs-vector-database distinction sharp; it's the misconception that lingers. Emphasize that grounding is their primary lever for trustworthy outputs and that chunking and metadata silently determine quality. They leave able to build and assess a RAG agent. Next week single agents become coordinated teams of agents — with a critic to keep them honest.

sections.courseJourney: This module scales from one agent to a coordinated team: a Coordinator that routes, specialists that execute, and a Validator/Critic that checks. It exists because real business processes decompose across roles, and because the critic pattern is how managers get reliability from non-deterministic agents. It follows RAG because specialists often need grounded knowledge to do their jobs.

"Doesn't every added agent add cost and latency?"
"How do I decide how to split responsibilities?"

A Validator/Critic is how you buy reliability from unreliable parts.
Each agent is still a simple loop; complexity lives in coordination.
More agents means more cost and failure surface.
Debugging multi-agent flows is a core operational skill.

Clarify it's often what makes the system trustworthy enough to ship.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: EMs arrive able to build a grounded single agent. Today they orchestrate teams of agents with a Coordinator and — crucially — a Validator/Critic that catches bad outputs. Emphasize the critic as reliability engineering, not decoration; it's how managers get dependable behavior from non-deterministic components.
