sections.oneMinuteRecap: This is managerial integration: EMs fuse the whole track into one operable system and, crucially, lead and justify its decisions. Coach for rationale — why this architecture, what it costs, where the evals and guardrails are, how reliable it is. Redirect complexity instincts toward retrieval and evaluation. Remind them the capstone is the story they'll retell as senior system-design answers in the next four deep dives. Reward defensible restraint over feature count. Next: four shared interview rehearsals at senior depth. EM Interview-Prep Deep Dives (Weeks 10–13) These four modules are identical in content to the SWE track's Weeks 12–15 and are written in full there. For EMs, the framing shifts from "can I build and defend this in code" to "can I lead, scope, and evaluate this as a system." Read the full SWE briefs and apply the EM delta below. EM W10 — Agentic Research Systems → see SWE Module 12. EM delta: emphasize scoping, memory/guardrail requirements, and productionization decisions a manager would own; lighter on implementation. EM W11 — Agentic Text-to-SQL → see SWE Module 13. EM delta: emphasize the reliability bar, cost math, and the risk of confidently-wrong queries against production data — a governance concern. EM W12 — Multi-Agent Coordination & Shared Intelligence → see SWE Module 14. EM delta: emphasize "when not to go multi-agent," coordination failure modes, and team/architecture tradeoffs. EM W13 — Self-Improving Agents: Evaluation & Verification Loops → see SWE Module 15. EM delta: emphasize verification strategy, LLM-as-judge governance, and continuous online evaluation as an operating practice. What EM learners already know (use in place of the SWE section 2 lists): builds from W1–W7 — the E-commerce Operations Agent; the RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent; the Trip Planner and multi-agent healthcare system; the Streamlit Audio Bot, ElevenLabs agent and Voice AI RAG app; the MCP/A2A ecosystem and Travel Weather Comparator; the Signup Email Agent (DeepEval, LangSmith, LLM-as-judge); and the LoRA ticket classifier with its TCO memo — plus their capstone (BRD-to-Engineering, Hiring Intelligence, Team Sentiment & Growth Feedback, or BYOP). They have not built SWE's LangGraph systems, hybrid search or QLoRA pipeline, so when a SWE brief cites a SWE project, reach for the nearest EM build — the Trip Planner or Travel Weather Comparator for coordination, the Signup Email Agent for evaluation, the ticket classifier for cost. The EM versions of W12–W13 also include EM Lens segments (phased delivery and SLAs, team ownership mirroring the agents, STAR incident stories); expect EMs to lean into those. Instructor note: because EMs experienced evaluation and ops as their core track (Week 6) rather than a late addition, they often engage these deep dives more comfortably than SWEs on the eval/ops phases and less comfortably on low-level architecture. Lean into their strength (evaluation, cost, reliability, governance) and scaffold the architecture phases more. TRACK 3 — Product Managers / TPMs (PMs–TPMs) The arc: PMs and TPMs learn the same agentic model as builders, but through a product lens and in no-code tools (Zapier, n8n, LangFlow). The path runs from a reflex→reasoning agent (W1) → grounded RAG agents (W2) → multi-agent orchestration with a critic (W3) → conversational/voice agents (W4) → AI Product Architecture, the track's pivot into RAG-vs-Agents-vs-Pipelines decision-making (W5) → evaluation and optimization (W6) → fine-tuning (W7), then a capstone and a heavily interview-focused final phase: Product Sense & Solution Fit (W10), Agentic System Design (W11), Evaluations/Safety/Governance (W12), and Production LLMOps (W13). Throughout, the question isn't "how do I build it" but "should we, what does it cost, how do we know it works, and how do I reason about it in a PM interview."

Why it matters to you as an instructor: PMs need enough technical literacy to earn credibility with engineers and to reason about tradeoffs — not to build production systems. sections.courseJourney: This module establishes what an agent actually is, so PMs can spec, scope, and evaluate agentic products rather than repeat buzzwords. sections.oneMinuteRecap: This is product integration under real constraints. PMs fuse the track into one system and, above all, defend its decisions — especially the Week 5 architecture choice. Coach relentlessly for rationale: why this architecture, what it costs, how it's evaluated, where the guardrails are, what the UX tradeoffs are. Redirect complexity instincts toward the right (often simpler) design and toward evaluation. Remind them every decision is future interview material. Reward defensible restraint. Next is the interview phase — four modules built to make them job-ready for AI PM/TPM roles. sections.courseJourney: This is the direct interview extension of Week 5, teaching PMs to design agentic systems layer by layer — Knowledge, Tools/Permissions/Guardrails, Agent Architecture, Observability — and to walk an interviewer through end-to-end designs. It exists because "design an agentic system for X" is the signature AI-PM/TPM interview question. It follows Product Sense because good system design starts from solution-fit framing.

concepts.label: W5
concepts.text: AI Product Architecture: Control, Execution and Reliability layers, design patterns, and RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines. W2–W6 — Layer ingredients: chunking, metadata filtering and grounding (W2); critic loops and routers (W3); scoped knowledge bases and prompt-level guardrails (W4); state, queues, isolation and graceful degradation (W5); and tracing and evaluation with LangFlow + Langfuse (W6).

concepts.label: W10
concepts.text: Product sense: the 5-filter AI vs Non-AI framework, L0/L1/L2 metrics, AI UX & Trust (visibility, verification, escape; friction calibrated to stakes), and the 9-category question bank.

sections.learnToday: Learners will be able to: frame an agentic system-design question; reason through the Knowledge Layer, the Tools/Permissions/Guardrails Layer, the Agent Architecture Layer, and the Observability Layer, each with an interview walkthrough (YouTube Creator Policy Assistant; Google Ads Campaign Agent; AI Coding Agent; Content-Moderation Agent); and handle end-to-end questions (Consumer Fintech Money Agent; Delivery Real-Time Order Recovery).
sections.preparesFor: The layered framework is the scaffold for the Governance (W12) and Production LLMOps (W13) interviews, which zoom into the observability/safety and production layers respectively.
connections: Frame the four layers as the structured version of Week 5's architecture thinking.
Map each layer to its origin: Knowledge=W2, Tools/Guardrails=W4–W5, Architecture=W3/W5, Observability=W6.
Use the walkthroughs as templates for the cadence of a live answer.
Preview that Week 12 drills into safety/governance and Week 13 into production.
Stress permissions as a PM-critical, often-forgotten layer.
likelyQuestions: "In what order should I cover the layers in an interview?"
"How much depth per layer in 45 minutes?"
"How do I handle permissions and guardrails as a PM?"
"What makes an end-to-end answer strong vs shallow?"
"How do I recover if I blank mid-design?"
teachingEmphasis: The four layers are a reusable design framework.
Every layer needs a stated tradeoff.
Permissions and guardrails are where PMs differentiate.
Observability is part of the design, not an afterthought.
End-to-end coherence beats depth in one layer.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify it's justified tradeoffs across layers.
Clarify PMs must design for it to ensure quality and trust.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This is the signature AI-PM interview skill: designing an agentic system, layer by layer, out loud. It's Week 5 turned into a rehearsable framework — Knowledge, Tools/Permissions/Guardrails, Agent Architecture, Observability — with four walkthroughs as templates. Map each layer to where it was learned so it's recall, not invention, and stress the layers PMs neglect (permissions, observability). Use the end-to-end questions to practice coherence over one-layer depth. This scaffolds the final two modules, which magnify the safety/governance and production layers into full interviews.

sections.courseJourney: This module drills the evaluation, safety, and governance reasoning that senior AI-PM interviews probe, entirely through case studies. It exists because as AI products gain autonomy, the ability to reason about what could go wrong and how you'd catch it becomes a defining PM competency. It follows System Design because governance is the layer that keeps a designed system safe in the world.

concepts.label: W11
concepts.text: Four-layer system design: Knowledge; Tools, Permissions & Guardrails (read/write/trigger gates, HITL on irreversible actions, Meta's Rule of Two); Agent Architecture (earn every extra agent, stopping conditions); Observability (health ≠ decision quality, drift, safety vs quality alerts) — with walkthroughs including an AI Coding Agent and a Content-Moderation Agent.

concepts.label: W10

sections.learnToday: Through five case-based question areas, learners will be able to: design evaluation systems (Alexa Shopping Agent); reason about metrics, thresholds & trust with audit checks (GitHub Copilot launch eval); ensure multi-agent reliability (5-Agent Travel Booking); reason about safety, autonomy & launch decisions (autonomous code-deployment agent, Devin); and debug/operate in production (customer-support agent CSAT drop). Each pairs an approach, concepts, and a case study.
sections.preparesFor: Governance reasoning is essential for senior AI-PM roles and complements Production LLMOps (W13). The debugging case (CSAT drop) directly bridges into production operations.
connections: Tie evaluation-system design to Week 6 and to the Critic pattern (W3).
Frame safety/autonomy decisions as the product form of HITL and guardrails.
Connect the CSAT-drop case to Week 13's production debugging.
Use each case to rehearse a structured approach: define good → set thresholds → catch failures → operate.
Emphasize launch-decision reasoning — go/no-go under uncertainty.
likelyQuestions: "How do I design an evaluation system from scratch in an interview?"
"How do I set thresholds without production data?"
"When is an autonomous agent safe enough to launch?"
"How do I debug a live quality regression like a CSAT drop?"
"How much autonomy should an agent have?"
teachingEmphasis: Evaluation design is a structured, teachable skill.
Thresholds and audits operationalize trust.
Autonomy and safety are launch-gating product decisions.
Production debugging starts from metrics and traces.
Case studies are rehearsal for real interview prompts.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify it's a core design and launch decision.
Clarify production monitoring (e.g. CSAT drops) is continuous governance.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This module makes governance concrete through five real-world cases — Alexa, Copilot, a 5-agent travel booker, Devin, and a CSAT regression. PMs learn to design evaluation systems, set trust thresholds, reason about autonomy and launch safety, and debug live regressions. Run each case as a structured rehearsal: define "good," set thresholds, anticipate failures, operate. Tie it back to Week 6 evaluation and the Critic pattern, and forward to Week 13's production focus. The maturity signal to instill is treating safety and autonomy as launch-gating product decisions, not compliance. One module remains: production LLMOps.

sections.courseJourney: The final module rehearses production reasoning — architecture, RAG-vs-fine-tuning, latency/cost, failure modes, and rollout — as senior interview questions. It exists because "how would you operate this in production" separates senior AI PMs from junior ones. It's last because it presumes all prior product, design, and governance reasoning.

sections.preparesFor: This is terminal interview preparation — the production layer of the System Design framework, expressed as a full interview. It ties together architecture, cost, evaluation, and governance into an operator's mindset.
connections: Frame it as the production layer of the Week 11 framework, zoomed in.
Tie RAG-vs-fine-tuning to Weeks 2 and 7 explicitly.
Connect failure-mode debugging to Week 12's CSAT case and Week 6 tracing.
Frame latency/cost tradeoffs as the product economics from Week 7.
Emphasize the operator's mindset: rollout, metrics, root-cause thinking.
likelyQuestions: "How do I choose RAG vs fine-tuning in an interview answer?"
"How do I reason about latency and cost tradeoffs concretely?"
"How do I debug a production failure from symptoms?"
"What does a strong rollout/launch plan sound like?"
"How technical should a PM be about production architecture?"
teachingEmphasis: Production reasoning is an operator's mindset PMs must show.
RAG vs fine-tuning is a recurring, decisive tradeoff.
Latency, cost, and quality are always in tension.
Failure diagnosis starts from metrics and the operational chain.
Rollout and metrics thinking signal seniority.

misconceptions.clarification: Clarify PMs must reason about operations to prioritize and derisk.

misconceptions.myth: RAG vs fine-tuning has one right answer.
misconceptions.clarification: Clarify it's context-dependent — defend the tradeoff.

sections.oneMinuteRecap: This closes the program with production reasoning framed as senior interview questions: architecture and the operational chain, RAG-vs-fine-tuning, latency/cost tradeoffs, and failure diagnosis. It's the production layer of the Week 11 framework, magnified. Tie every thread back — RAG (W2), fine-tuning (W7), tracing (W6), the CSAT case (W12) — so learners see it as synthesis, not new material. The mindset to send them out with is the operator's: think in rollouts, metrics, tradeoffs, and root causes. From here they're rehearsing a complete, coherent story — from product sense to system design to governance to production — ready for AI PM/TPM interviews.
